Title: So how is V:TES doing business-wise---LSJ?

Messages.Author: Menno Rieff
Messages.Body:
I would be very interested to know how the financial performance has
been of V:TES for White Wolf. Questions like the following come to
mind:

Are the sales levels satisfying?
Are costs equal to planned budgets?
Is V:TES operating at a profit?
Did one expansion outperform the other?
Is White Wolf overall happy to feature V:TES?

Can any information be given about these issues?
If it is undesirable to mention specific numbers, some more vague
expressions like "Yes, we are currently making money" and "No, we
expected higher sales for expansion X" will do.

Just curious!
Menno

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


VTES has been doing fine for White Wolf.

The second print run of Sabbat War is virtually sold out at the
White Wolf level (the distributors and retailers may still have
some stock left).

Both Final Nights and Bloodlines have sold at the break-even point
or better, although they have not sold as well as Sabbat War.

However, the biggest test for the long term of V:TES will come this
summer with the new editio of the base set. Eventually any game will
fade away without new players, and a new edition focused on the most
popular clans is going to be V:TES's best (and in some ways only)
shot at significantly expanding its player base for several years to
come.

--
LSJ (vte...@white-wolf.com) V:TES Net.Rep for White Wolf, Inc.
Links to revised rulebook, rulings, errata, and tournament rules:
http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/

I did not come to Jyhad from V:tM. The idea of role-playing a vampire is, as a
theme, just a bit too creepy for my taste. Playing vampires in a competitive
card game doesn't bother me because one does not have to take it as seriously.

>> Traditions and b) cheaper cards. !Brujah, !Malk, Assamite, Setites,

The people most commonly encountered in tournament and casual play are typical
of the people V:tES has already attracted, not necessarily the people they are
trying to attract. In particular, these include people who have been attracted
to the game specifically BY the Sabbat and Independent expansions.

But it seems to me that it goes without saying that a game that focusses on
vampires as its heroes and main characters, and bloodsucking as its theme, will
not have universal appeal. At least some people will find the theme too
unpleasant to enjoy, and some might even find it offensive.

It also seems to me logical, that if you shift the focus to clans that are
inhuman and depraved even by Vampire standards, you are going to narrow the
appeal still further. This is essentially what has happened with the Sabbat
and Independent expansions.

In theory, at least, the theme of the V:tM RPG is about fighting against one's
vampire nature and preserving one's humanity. The seven clans of the Camarilla
are the ones whose members are usually portrayed as the most human and
sympathetic. The others range from the wierd alien-ness of the independents,
to the in-your-face depravity of the Sabbat.

-- John Whelan

It doesn't seem to lower the appeal much. You're the first person I've seen
who avoids Sabbat because of the backstory. Tribute to the Master grossed
me out when I first saw it but I don't think about the art anymore and all
are in decks. To be honest, many of the Sabbat clans seems eeeevil only
if you know the backstory. Lasombra, !Ven, !Nos, !Brujah, and !Gangrel
don't seem any worse than their Cam brethren just on a card basis. !Malks
wouldn't be different if the +Malks had Dem, which I expect the new ones
will. !Tor, !Trem, and Tzi - OK, they're pretty creepy.

>In theory, at least, the theme of the V:tM RPG is about fighting against one's
>vampire nature and preserving one's humanity. The seven clans of the
Camarilla
>are the ones whose members are usually portrayed as the most human and
>sympathetic. The others range from the wierd alien-ness of the independents,
>to the in-your-face depravity of the Sabbat.
>

Righto. The question is, how many of those who know and care will play
the game? I think it makes sense for WW to try to draw role-players into
V:tES, but I don't expect it to work. I think the market's pretty much what
you see now, and I think the Cam set would increase the market by 50%
at most and probably less. It also *might* sell rather poorly in itself -
I, and many of the other active players, have a gazillion Jyhad cards.
I've no need for new ones unless they are a) all different [very hard]
or b) escalate [in which case I'd be furious and not buy any anyway].
A well-balanced, part-reprint Cam set would be lower on my priority
list than SW until I've got several more boxes of SW.

If WW wants to bring in new players from V:tM I think the #1 top priority
is a full set of good starter decks and links to Jyhad/V:tES base set sellers
on the WW page. The learning curve needs to be cut down. To make
a good deck takes well over a box w/o trading and newbies are unlikely
to want to make lots of trades until they have some grasp of how things
work. It makes sense for WW to wait until they have their own
Cam set to sell, so they capture the sales, but I don't think that having
a 2nd Cam set will help much in and of itself.

PS I'd love to be wrong about the market size.

An initial investment in a CCG, IMO, will always involve multiple boxes. If

require gifting the appropriate rares to make a good deck.

>It makes sense for WW to wait until they have their own

I don't think so either. At best, a new base set provides an easier entry into
the game than other sets and fills some sort of need. Thing is, the need being
fulfilled with the new Cam set doesn't seem to be a particularly important one
given how much Jyhad/V:TES has been printed. Don't want to wait until it dries
up completely, though, or you leave a window for people to be frustrated by the
lack of a base set. Do want to print a bunch to prevent having stocks of the
latest base set be hard to acquire.

>PS I'd love to be wrong about the market size.

It's hard for me to imagine that there's some relatively large untapped player
base out there. For some CCGs, including far less successful ones, I could.
The way I'd envision gaining more players is through friends who play. So,
best thing to do is try and prevent those friends from leaving. In other
words, don't overly irritate your existing base.

I'd expect the Cam set to be a necessary hit to set up profitability with
future expansions. If so, what's important is surviving the hit.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Halcyan 2 wrote:

> cur...@aol.com wrote:
> > The learning curve needs to be cut down.

> I really don't want to see a "dumbing down" of the rules like from Jyhad -->
> VTES.

> I don't know about the rest of you, but I *like* the complexity and intricacies
> of the game. It might be a bit steeper of a learning curve for new players, but
> once they begin to get it, I'm sure they'll also appreciate all of the
> subtleties of the game.

There are "good complexities" and "bad complexities". Good ones don't need to be
learned as rules - they appear as wrinkles and subtle choices in strategies. Bad
complexities are those that add nothing to strategy but simply confuse players -
not just new ones but all of us - as to how to play the game by rules. Granted,
the good complexities often come at the cost of accepting the bad ones but it is
by no means a given thing. In fact, my highest admiration for game designers go
to the guys who have a sense for how to create interesting strategy choices within
the framework of a simple, eloquent game design. When I've designed games in the
past, I've often been struck by how much I can improve them with a pair of scissors
as opposed to a marking pencil: get rid of the excess, stupid, overdesigned fat
and what's left is often quite good.

You really should not have any argument with Ian's statement. Ideally, we wouldn't
have to dumb down _the game_ by simplifying certain rules.

Fred

My history with the game goes like this:
1) Huge fascination with vampire mythology since early childhood
2) Coming across a box of Jyhad while in a game store for something other
than games
3) Buying a bunch of Jyhad boxes for my friends as X-Mas gifts so I would
have people to play with
4) Discovering that the game was based on an RPG (something I had avoided
since grade 9 when I discovered girls)
5) Buying the Ventrue and Brujah clanbooks to find out more about the world
the cards inhabited
6) Discovering that there were people who met in a park in Windsor to play
'live-action' vampire games
7) Deciding that I wanted to test my improvisational acting skills and meet
kewl goth chicks
8) Eventually... years later, I tried the pen-and-paper RPG after much
resistance to the idea
9) Playing V:tM online in New Bremen (White Wolf's chat room) until I was
banned for being a 'problem player'
10) Strong aversion to any form of RPG, whether live or pen-and-paper,
unless I am positive that the people I play with are not twinks, morons or
criminally insane.
11) Re-discovery of the CCG after White Wolf takes over (along with a
realization that we were playing everything *very* wrong)
12) At some point I became the best Jyhad player in the world... but you all
know that already.

> As for the Sabbat, however, I find them far more interesting in both the
RPG
> and CCG. Can't relate to their philosophies in the RPG, but Camarilla =
dull.
> Doesn't help that the Camarilla is only 7 clans where the Sabbat is about
13.
> Nor does it help that the Sabbat have two extra exclusive disciplines,
both of
> which do interesting things.

I agree. Thematically, the Sabbat appeals to me far more than the
Vanilla-Camarilla. I enjoy the whole descent into depravity thing as much as
the next guy, but the Sabbat in general has themes that appeal to me far
more. While I don't really enjoy the ultra-violence aspect, I do enjoy the
Sabbat for its inherently anarchistic (in a bad way) structure and its
history and conflict. I enjoy their mock-religious rites and their view of
history as one big conflict against the Antedilluveans and their pawns.

The Camarilla bores me mostly. I always liked the Gangrel though, but then
look what happened to them. They got bored of the Cam too.

> As for the Independents, I find them much more interesting in the RPG, at
least
> nowadays.

Yeah. I've always thought that they made for more interesting antagonists to
the Camarilla than the Sabbat did. The Sabbat is good for a team-vs-team
rumble but how does one deal with slow corruption or ghostly spies or
assassination attempts or illusions? These can add up to some very
intriguing conflicts and scenarios.

I just wish it was possible to play the game with people who weren't weenies
(and I don't mean small caps).

Cheers,
WES

Probably true. But a terrible deal if you want to expand the player base.
People start games as poor students, mostly, and then grow up to gainfully

novels. V:tES currently serves only the latter market which IMO is a big

Magic, and the increase in $$ less essential for a successful deck but
still great for variety, flexibility, showing off, etc. I'd like to think
this could make money for WW while not being as brutally exploitive

There are certainly more poor student game players than well-off
adult game players. More importantly, that's where recruitment is
most promising, when social networks are looser, when you meet
a lot of new people , when you try more new things. It's just
that those students don't play Jyhad. In a few years, they'll be
employed adults with money - but they probably still won't play
Jyhad, they'll spend their money on something else.

Jyhad/V:tES is very friendly to *skilled* poor players because it's
done well with the great rare problem. But it's hostile to newbie
poor players because there are so many different categories and
such a complexity of balancing. We will all benefit if that is addressed
well; more players, more cards, more discussions, more ideas.

Think of it this way. Most of us who missed the very beginning
started by borrowing decent decks from player friends. Decks
that had good balance, enough Wakes and Blood Dolls, and came
with a little advice on how to play it. Probably decks that were
easy to play; not one with Masks and Change of Target and
complicated condition cards. I'm suggesting we put those decks
in packages with "Starter" on them and sell them for $10 of
whatever so anybody can start playing.

>Magic has the marketing

>stop at $30 and have fun as long as you avoid the suitcases.

I'm not sure why you think Magic makes you believe you can have a playable deck
for $30. If I spent $30 on Magic cards and tried to put a deck together, I'd
get utterly stomped by anyone with a real deck. A tournament deck requires
about 2-3 boxes of every expansion that is legal in the format. And, Magic has
pretty much become a tournament game.

The only way to compete with a $30 purchase is to play a sealed deck tournament
or two draft tournaments or get into a sealed league. I'm currently playing in
a sealed league that's potentially free, though in order for that, you have to
have an existing collection. An article on it might be in issue #50 of Scrye.

The advantage Magic has, in terms of ease of entry, is that limited play is
huge. Anyone can plop down $20-25 and "compete" in a sealed tournament. Can
completely ignore constructed like I have for ages (once it became clear that
is was a ridiculous amount of money to have the cards to compete in
constructed). Where limited in most CCGs is a break from the routine or is
just plain bad, it is sufficiently fresh in Magic to be the only way to play.

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
cur...@aol.com writes:

>I'm not sure why you think Magic makes you believe you can have a playable
deck
>for $30. If I spent $30 on Magic cards and tried to put a deck together, I'd
>get utterly stomped by anyone with a real deck. A tournament deck requires
>about 2-3 boxes of every expansion that is legal in the format. And, Magic
>has pretty much become a tournament game.

With $30 or so you can make a passable 2-color deck. You have enough land,
you have enough spells, and you can play any spell in your deck with your land.
You'll even get to pick and choose somewhat amongst your color-appropriate
stuff. This is exactly what I did when I started, and while I lost more than I
won, I did win often enough to want to continue. To get an analogous monoclan
library, you'd need about 3 of each common for 20+ or so of each discipline
(remember, your average V:tES library card is less likely to be usable in any
given deck due to combo requirements). I don't know the new distribution, but
that's got to be more than a box.

Big purchase requirements scare people off. From when I was just starting, I
remember one girl who showed up with a Toreador deck. She played V:tM and
liked Tor and I think she'd brought her boyfriend with her. When she realized
every decent deck should have 4-6 Wakes she said she wasn't interested if she
had to buy that many cards to play one deck. (Obviously she must have traded
to the Tor deck.) Never saw her, or the guy she came with, ever again. And
that's exactly WW's target expansion market.

>The advantage Magic has, in terms of ease of entry, is that limited play is
>huge. Anyone can plop down $20-25 and "compete" in a sealed tournament.

Limited is a good format for bringing people into the game too. James is
running an OnTE league and getting in new players. Jyhad just isn't suitable
for limited; but we need an alternative.

To some extent the appearance of playability in a $30 Magic deck is deceptive.
It plays the way a Magic deck should, but it's a great deal weaker than a tuned
deck. Nonetheless, it looks good enough to a beginner, it's not going to be a
complete joke even in a serious group, and if your friends are in the same boat
everything will be fine.

A tournament-only game is not enough. If Magic is down to tournament-only (I
don't play it anymore) it's on the way out.
